examples.en: Livestock farming is well developed in this region.
My father is in the livestock business.
The price of livestock products went up a lot.
He studied animal husbandry at university.
I hear livestock farmers have a lot of worries.
There was news about livestock farms on TV.

explain: 축산은 소, 돼지, 닭을 키워서 고기나 우유, 달걀을 얻는 일을 통틀어 말해요. 뉴스나 신문에서는 '축산업', '축산물', '축산 농가'처럼 뒤에 말을 붙여 자주 써요. 식물을 키우는 일은 '농사'나 '재배'라고 해서 구별해요.
explain_en: Chuksan is the general word for raising cattle, pigs, or chickens for meat, milk, and eggs. In news and papers it usually appears with a following word, as in 축산업, 축산물, and 축산 농가. Growing plants is called 농사 or 재배, so the two are kept apart.

examples.en: Popular items sell out quickly.
I tried to order it, but it was already sold out.
These shoes will be sold out by tomorrow.
Will the sold-out book come back in stock?
Most things sold out on the first day of the sale, which was a pity.
We ran out of stock and it ended up sold out.

explain: 쇼핑몰에서 상품 옆에 '품절'이라고 쓰여 있으면 지금 살 수 없다는 표시예요. 가게 주인이 말할 때는 '다 팔렸어요', '재고가 없어요'라고도 해요. 다시 들어오면 '재입고'라고 부르니 같이 알아 두면 좋아요.
explain_en: On a shopping site, 품절 next to an item means you cannot buy it right now. A shop owner speaking aloud may also say 다 팔렸어요 or 재고가 없어요. When it comes back in stock it is called 재입고, which is worth learning together.

examples.en: The complications of diabetes are scary.

examples.ko: 수술 뒤에 합병증이 생기지 않아서 다행이에요.
examples.en: I am glad no complications appeared after the surgery.

examples.ko: 감기를 오래 두면 합병증으로 이어질 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you leave a cold alone for long, it can lead to complications.
The doctor told me to watch out for complications.

examples.ko: 할아버지는 합병증 때문에 한 달 더 입원하셨어요.
examples.en: My grandfather stayed in the hospital another month because of complications.

examples.ko: 합병증을 막으려면 꾸준히 약을 먹어야 해요.
examples.en: To prevent complications, you have to keep taking your medicine.

explain: 합병증은 한 병 때문에 다른 병이나 증상이 따라서 생기는 것이에요. '합병증이 생기다', '합병증을 막다', '합병증이 오다'처럼 써요. '당뇨 합병증'처럼 병 이름과 붙여 많이 말해요.
explain_en: Hapbyeongjeung is a second illness or symptom that follows from a first illness. It pairs with 생기다, 막다, and 오다, as in 합병증이 생기다. It is often attached to a disease name, as in 당뇨 합병증.

examples.ko: 우리 집 꼬맹이가 벌써 학교에 가요.
examples.en: The little one in our house already goes to school.
I am amazed that little kid has grown this big.
Little kids are running around in the park.

examples.ko: 꼬맹이 때 사진을 보면 웃음이 나요.
examples.en: I laugh when I see photos from when I was a little kid.
I gave some snacks to the little kid next door.
Our youngest is still just a little kid.

explain: 꼬맹이는 작은 아이를 귀엽게, 조금 장난스럽게 부르는 말이에요. 친구나 가족끼리 편하게 쓰고, 어른에게나 공식적인 자리에서는 '어린이', '아이'라고 해요. 비슷한 말로 '꼬마'도 있어요.
explain_en: Kkomaengi is an affectionate, slightly playful name for a small child. Friends and family use it casually; in formal settings people say 어린이 or 아이 instead. 꼬마 is a similar word.

examples.en: My wallet was stolen on the subway yesterday.
My bike was stolen, so I went to the police station.
I still haven't found the stolen bag.

examples.ko: 차 안에 물건을 두면 도난당할 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you leave things in the car, they can be stolen.
I hear phone thefts happen often.
After the theft I put a lock on the door.

explain: 도난당하다는 내 물건을 누가 훔쳐 가서 잃었을 때 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '잃어버리다'는 내 실수로 없앤 것이고, '도난당하다'나 '도둑맞다'는 누가 훔친 것이라서 달라요. '도둑맞다'가 말할 때 더 자연스럽고, 도난당하다는 뉴스나 신고할 때 많이 써요.
explain_en: Donandanghada is used when someone stole your belongings. 잃어버리다 means you lost it through your own mistake, while 도난당하다 and 도둑맞다 mean someone took it. 도둑맞다 sounds more natural in speech, and 도난당하다 is common in news and police reports.

en: keep in mind; take to heart

examples.en: I will definitely keep what you said in mind.
Please be sure to keep this point in mind.

examples.ko: 처음 일을 시작할 때 들은 조언을 아직도 명심해요.
examples.en: I still keep in mind the advice I heard when I started working.
I made a point of not repeating the mistake.
More people take the safety rules to heart now.
I set off to study abroad with my parents' words in mind.

explain: 명심하다는 중요한 말이나 교훈을 잊지 않고 마음에 새긴다는 느낌이에요. 보통 윗사람의 조언이나 경고를 들은 뒤 '명심하겠습니다', '명심할게요'라고 대답해요. '기억하다'는 그냥 안 잊는 것이고, 명심하다는 앞으로 행동에 반영하겠다는 다짐이 들어 있어요.
explain_en: Myeongsimhada means to take something important in your heart so you do not forget it. It is the usual reply to advice or a warning from someone senior, as in 명심할게요. 기억하다 just means not forgetting, while 명심하다 carries a promise to act on it.

examples.en: That reporter critiques movies sharply.

examples.ko: 친구의 그림을 비평해 달라는 부탁을 받았어요.
examples.en: I was asked to give feedback on my friend's painting.

examples.ko: 남의 작품을 비평하기는 쉬워도 만들기는 어려워요.
examples.en: It is easy to critique others' work but hard to make your own.
A critic reviewed the new novel.

examples.ko: 비평하는 글을 쓸 때는 근거가 필요해요.
examples.en: When writing a critical piece, you need evidence.
They criticized the policy and also offered an alternative.

explain: 비평하다는 책, 영화, 그림 같은 작품이나 정책의 좋은 점과 나쁜 점을 따져서 평가하는 일이에요. 단순히 나쁘게 말하는 '비난하다'와 달리 이유를 들어 분석한다는 느낌이에요. '평가하다'보다 글이나 말로 의견을 내놓는 쪽에 가까워요.
explain_en: Bipyeonghada means to judge the good and bad points of a work, such as a book, film, or policy, giving reasons. Unlike 비난하다, which is plain blame, it implies analysis. Compared with 평가하다, it leans toward stating an opinion in writing or speech.

examples.ko: 모든 일에는 좋은 면과 나쁜 면, 양면이 있어요.
examples.en: Everything has two sides, a good one and a bad one.

examples.ko: 이 종이는 양면에 인쇄할 수 있어요.
examples.en: You can print on both sides of this paper.
I stuck the photo down with double-sided tape.

examples.ko: 문제를 한쪽만 보지 말고 양면을 살펴보세요.
examples.en: Don't look at only one side of a problem; look at both.
The internet has two sides, convenience and danger.

examples.ko: 양면 복사를 하면 종이를 아낄 수 있어요.
examples.en: Copying on both sides saves paper.

explain: 양면은 물건의 앞뒤, 또는 어떤 일의 좋은 점과 나쁜 점처럼 서로 다른 두 쪽을 함께 말할 때 써요. 물건에는 '양면 테이프', '양면 복사'처럼 붙여 쓰고, 생각을 말할 때는 '양면이 있다'로 자주 써요.
explain_en: Yangmyeon refers to two different sides together, such as the front and back of an object or the good and bad of a situation. For objects it appears in 양면 테이프 and 양면 복사; for ideas, 양면이 있다 is common.

examples.en: Rain is forecast across the country tomorrow.
Snow has been forecast for the weekend.
A typhoon was forecast, so I put off my trip.
The rain started earlier than the forecast time.

examples.ko: 한파가 예보될 때는 옷을 따뜻하게 입어요.
examples.en: When a cold wave is forecast, I dress warmly.
Strong winds are forecast from the afternoon.

explain: 예보되다는 날씨나 재해가 미리 알려졌다는 뜻으로 주로 날씨 뉴스에서 써요. '비가 예보되어 있다', '폭설이 예보됐다'처럼 날씨 말과 같이 나와요. 사람이 일부러 알리는 건 '예보하다', 알려진 결과를 말하는 건 예보되다예요.
explain_en: Yebodoeda is used mostly in weather news for something that has been announced ahead of time, as in 비가 예보되어 있다. 예보하다 is the person or agency doing the announcing, while 예보되다 describes the result that has been announced. It sits next to weather words such as rain, snow, and typhoon.

examples.en: That kind of behaviour is never tolerated.

examples.ko: 약속 시간에 늦는 건 용납되기 어려워요.
examples.en: Being late for an appointment is hard to accept.
Lies are not tolerated at school.

examples.ko: 이 정도 실수는 용납될 수 있어요.
examples.en: A mistake of this size can be tolerated.

examples.ko: 예전에는 용납됐던 일도 지금은 문제가 돼요.
examples.en: Things that used to be accepted are now a problem.
A society where discrimination is tolerated is not healthy.

explain: 용납되다는 '용납하다'의 피동 표현으로, 어떤 행동이 허용되고 받아들여질 때 써요. 대부분 '용납되지 않다'나 '용납될 수 없다'처럼 부정형으로 말해요. '허용되다'가 규칙상 가능하다는 느낌이라면 용납되다는 도덕적으로 봐줄 수 있느냐에 가까워요.
explain_en: Yongnapdoeda is the passive form of 용납하다, used when an action gets allowed or accepted. It is most often used in the negative, as in 용납되지 않다 or 용납될 수 없다. 허용되다 feels like rule-based permission, while 용납되다 is closer to whether it can be excused morally.

examples.en: I can't tolerate people who lie.

examples.ko: 부모님은 늦게 들어오는 걸 용납하지 않으세요.
examples.en: My parents don't tolerate coming home late.

examples.ko: 한 번의 실수는 용납할 수 있어요.
examples.en: I can forgive one mistake.

examples.ko: 회사는 그런 행동을 용납하지 않겠다고 밝혔어요.
examples.en: The company said it would not tolerate that behaviour.

examples.ko: 내가 용납한 적도 없는데 왜 그래요?
examples.en: I never accepted it, so why are you acting like this?
It is hard to put up with even rude language.

explain: 용납하다는 잘못이나 마음에 안 드는 일을 참고 받아들인다는 뜻으로, 보통 '용납하지 않다', '용납할 수 없다'처럼 못 받아들인다는 단호한 말에 써요. '참다'는 불편해도 견딘다는 느낌이고, 용납하다는 그 행동 자체를 허락한다는 점이 달라요. 말할 때보다 글이나 공식적인 자리에서 더 자주 써요.
explain_en: Yongnaphada means accepting something wrong or unwelcome, and it usually shows up in firm refusals like 용납하지 않다 or 용납할 수 없다. 참다 is enduring discomfort, while 용납하다 is actually permitting the behaviour. It appears more in writing and formal settings than in casual talk.

examples.en: He couldn't stand people's mockery.
The mocking tone bothered me.

examples.ko: 실수한 친구를 조롱의 대상으로 삼으면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not make a friend who made a mistake a target of ridicule.
The comments were full of mockery, which upset me.
That remark was mockery, not praise.
Because of the ridicule, she left school.

explain: 조롱은 상대를 우습게 만들려고 놀리고 비웃는 말이나 행동이에요. '놀림'은 가볍게 장난으로 할 수도 있지만, 조롱은 상대를 깎아내리려는 나쁜 의도가 분명해서 훨씬 무거운 말이에요. '조롱을 당하다', '조롱의 대상'처럼 써요.
explain_en: Jorong is words or acts meant to make someone look foolish by laughing at them. 놀림 can be light teasing, but 조롱 clearly intends to belittle and is a much heavier word. It is used in phrases like 조롱을 당하다 and 조롱의 대상.

examples.en: His friends mocked his pronunciation.
Don't say things that mock other people.

examples.ko: 그 광고는 노인을 조롱한다는 비판을 받았어요.
examples.en: That advertisement was criticised for mocking the elderly.
People mocked and laughed at him after he failed.
It caused a big controversy because someone mocked the player.
She spoke with a mocking smile.

explain: 조롱하다는 상대를 깔보면서 비웃고 놀리는 것이에요. '놀리다'는 친한 사이에서도 가볍게 쓰지만, 조롱하다는 존중이 없는 나쁜 행동이라 분위기가 심각해요. '비웃다'보다 말과 행동으로 적극적으로 우습게 만든다는 느낌이 강해요.
explain_en: Jorounghada means looking down on someone while laughing at them. 놀리다 can be light teasing between friends, but 조롱하다 shows no respect and sounds serious. Compared with 비웃다, it feels more active, as if words and actions are used to make the person look ridiculous.

examples.en: I saw a big trailer truck on the highway.
The trailer truck is heading to the port with cargo.
My uncle drives a trailer truck.

examples.ko: 뒤에 트레일러가 붙은 차는 속도가 느려요.
examples.en: A vehicle with a trailer attached is slower.
The road was blocked because of a trailer accident.
We rented a camping trailer and travelled.

explain: 트레일러는 짐을 싣기 위해 트럭 뒤에 연결하는 큰 차량이에요. 한국에서는 짐을 싣는 큰 트럭을 말할 때 가장 많이 쓰고, 캠핑카처럼 뒤에 끌고 다니는 '캠핑 트레일러'도 있어요. 영화 예고편을 뜻하는 'trailer'는 한국어로 보통 '예고편'이라고 해서 구별해요.
explain_en: A teureilleo is a large vehicle attached behind a truck to carry cargo. In Korea it mostly refers to big cargo trucks, though a 캠핑 트레일러 pulled behind a car also exists. A movie trailer is usually called 예고편, which keeps the two meanings apart.

examples.en: Milk is a food with a high calcium content.
The ingredient label shows the amount of sugar.
I want to buy a product that contains vitamins.
Check the ingredients carefully.
We need to test whether it contains lead.

examples.ko: 이 제품은 색소 함유량이 0%라서 아이도 쓸 수 있어요.
examples.en: This product has 0% colouring content, so children can use it too.

explain: 함유는 어떤 성분이 안에 들어 있는 것을 말하는데, 주로 식품이나 화장품 포장, 설명서 같은 글에 나와요. '함유량', '함유 성분'처럼 뒤에 말이 붙는 경우가 많아요. 말할 때는 '들어 있다'가 훨씬 자연스러워요.
explain_en: Hamyu means a substance is contained inside, and it appears mainly in writing such as food or cosmetics packaging and manuals. It often takes a following word, as in 함유량 or 함유 성분. In speech, 들어 있다 sounds far more natural.

examples.en: Spinach contains a lot of iron.
This product contains natural ingredients.
I eat fruit containing vitamins every day.
I picked a snack that has no artificial colouring.

examples.ko: 이 물은 미네랄을 함유해서 맛이 부드러워요.
examples.en: This water contains minerals, so it tastes smooth.
The more sugar something contains, the higher its calories.

explain: 함유하다는 안에 어떤 성분을 가지고 있다는 뜻의 글말이에요. 말할 때는 '들어 있다'를 쓰고, 설명서나 광고, 뉴스에서 함유하다를 많이 봐요. '포함하다'는 여러 항목 중 하나로 넣는 것이고, 함유하다는 물질이 성분으로 들어 있을 때 써요.
explain_en: Hamyuhada is a written-style verb meaning something holds a substance as an ingredient. In speech people say 들어 있다, while manuals, ads, and news use 함유하다. 포함하다 is counting something as one item in a group, whereas 함유하다 is for a substance present as a component.

examples.en: My friend is holding a solo exhibition next month.
I went to the painter's first solo exhibition.

examples.ko: 개인전에서는 한 사람의 작품만 볼 수 있어요.
examples.en: At a solo show you can see only one person's works.
He won the gold medal in the individual table tennis event.
This tournament is split into team and individual events.

examples.ko: 개인전 준비로 요즘 잠을 거의 못 자요.
examples.en: I hardly sleep these days preparing for my solo show.

explain: 개인전은 두 가지로 써요. 미술에서는 한 작가의 작품만 모은 전시회이고, 운동에서는 팀이 아닌 한 사람이 겨루는 경기예요. 반대말은 전시회에서는 여럿이 함께 여는 '단체전', 경기에서도 '단체전'이에요.
explain_en: Gaeinjeon has two uses: in art it is an exhibition of one artist's work, and in sports it is a match where one person competes rather than a team. The opposite in both cases is 단체전, a group show or team event.

examples.en: Nights living alone can sometimes feel lonely.
He lived a solitary life.

examples.ko: 사람들 속에 있어도 고독할 때가 있어요.
examples.en: Even among people there are times I feel alone.

examples.ko: 산 위에 서 있는 나무가 고독해 보였어요.
examples.en: The tree standing on the mountain looked lonely.
This song has a lonely and desolate mood.
The first year studying abroad was truly lonely.

explain: 고독하다는 곁에 사람이 없어서 느끼는 쓸쓸함, 또는 혼자라는 상태를 깊이 느끼는 감정이에요. '외롭다'는 일상에서 누구나 쓰는 말이고, 고독하다는 소설이나 노래 가사처럼 좀 더 무겁고 문학적인 느낌이에요. 친구에게 말할 때는 '외로워요'가 더 자연스러워요.
explain_en: Godokhada is the deep feeling of loneliness from having no one beside you, or from being alone. 외롭다 is the everyday word anyone uses, while 고독하다 feels heavier and more literary, like in novels and song lyrics. To a friend, 외로워요 sounds more natural.

examples.en: I went to the baseball park at the weekend.

examples.ko: 새 구장이 다음 달에 문을 열어요.
examples.en: The new ballpark opens next month.
We agreed to meet in front of the stadium.
The grass at this ballpark is really beautiful.

examples.ko: 우리 동네에는 작은 축구 구장이 있어요.
examples.en: There is a small football ground in our neighbourhood.

examples.ko: 구장 안에서 먹는 치킨이 제일 맛있어요.
examples.en: Chicken eaten inside the ballpark tastes best.

explain: 구장은 야구나 축구처럼 공으로 하는 경기를 하는 곳이에요. 한국에서는 특히 야구장을 말할 때 많이 써서 '잠실 구장'처럼 불러요. 축구는 '축구장'이나 '경기장'이라고도 하고, 아주 큰 경기장은 '스타디움'이라고 하기도 해요.
explain_en: Gujang is a place where ball games such as baseball or football are played. In Korea it is used especially for baseball parks, as in 잠실 구장. Football grounds are also called 축구장 or 경기장, and very large ones 스타디움.

examples.en: The workers held a sit-in in front of the factory.
Students are staging a sit-in at the president's office.
The sit-in has been going on for ten days.
The residents began a sit-in in opposition to the construction.
The sit-in didn't stop even in cold weather.
Citizens sent food to the sit-in tent.

explain: 농성은 자기 주장을 알리려고 한곳에 자리를 잡고 계속 머무르는 시위예요. '농성을 하다', '농성에 들어가다', '농성 중이다'처럼 써요. 길을 걸으며 하는 '행진'이나 구호를 외치는 '시위'와 달리 같은 장소에서 오래 머문다는 점이 특징이에요.
explain_en: Nongseong is a protest where people settle in one place and stay to make their point. Typical forms are 농성을 하다, 농성에 들어가다, and 농성 중이다. Unlike a march (행진) or a rally with slogans (시위), the key feature is staying in the same place for a long time.

examples.en: He made it big as a singer.
If you work hard, you will succeed big someday.

examples.ko: 어릴 때부터 재능이 있어서 대성할 줄 알았어요.
examples.en: He had talent from childhood, so I knew he'd go far.
To achieve great success, you need perseverance.
He is someone who left home and made it big in Seoul.

examples.ko: 대성하고 나서도 처음 마음을 잊지 않았어요.
examples.en: Even after becoming a great success, he did not forget his first resolve.

explain: 대성하다는 일이나 분야에서 크게 성공해 이름을 얻는다는 뜻이에요. 보통 미래에 대한 응원이나 덕담으로 '대성하세요', '대성할 거예요'라고 말해요. 그냥 '성공하다'보다 훨씬 크게 이루었다는 느낌이고, 주로 사람에게 쓰며 가수, 선수, 학자 같은 직업 이야기에 많이 나와요.
explain_en: Daeseonghada means to succeed greatly and make a name for yourself in a field. It often appears in good wishes about the future, such as 대성하세요. It feels much bigger than plain 성공하다, and it is used for people, especially singers, athletes, and scholars.

examples.en: I suffered damage because my ID was misused.

examples.ko: 도용 피해를 입은 사람이 늘고 있어요.
examples.en: The number of people who suffered misuse is growing.

examples.ko: 도용 사실이 밝혀져서 큰 문제가 됐어요.
examples.en: It became a big problem when the unauthorised use came to light.

examples.ko: 개인정보 도용을 막으려면 비밀번호를 자주 바꾸세요.
examples.en: To prevent identity misuse, change your password often.
The artist protested about the unauthorised use of the picture.
If someone uses your card without permission, you must report it right away.

explain: 도용은 남의 이름, 카드, 정보, 그림 같은 것을 허락 없이 자기 것처럼 쓰는 일이에요. 뉴스와 안내문에서 '신분 도용', '카드 도용', '사진 도용'처럼 많이 보여요. '훔치다'는 물건을 가져가는 것이고, 도용은 가져가지 않아도 몰래 써서 피해를 주는 것까지 포함해요.
explain_en: Doyong is using someone else's name, card, information, or image without permission as if it were yours. It is common in news and notices, as in 신분 도용 and 카드 도용. 훔치다 is taking an object, while 도용 includes using something secretly without removing it, which still causes harm.

en: be misused; be used without permission

examples.en: My photo was used in an ad without permission.
My card was misused, so I called the bank.
I found out later that my name had been misused.
I changed my password so my account wouldn't be hijacked.
I worry my work will be copied without permission.
Incidents of ID numbers being misused are rising.

explain: 도용되다는 내 이름, 사진, 카드 같은 것을 누가 허락 없이 써서 피해를 입는 상황에서 써요. 피해자 입장에서 '내 계정이 도용됐어요'처럼 말하는 경우가 많아요. 가해자 쪽에서 말할 때는 '도용하다'를 써요.
explain_en: Doyongdoeda describes the victim's side when your name, photo, or card is used without permission, as in 내 계정이 도용됐어요. The person who does it is described with 도용하다.

examples.en: Someone used my name without permission.
You must not use other people's photos without permission.

examples.ko: 그는 친구의 아이디어를 도용해서 상을 받았어요.
examples.en: He used a friend's idea and won a prize.
The person who used someone else's card was caught.
There was an attempt to hijack the account.
They used the logo without permission and didn't apologise.

explain: 도용하다는 남의 이름, 카드, 사진, 아이디어를 허락 없이 자기 것처럼 쓰는 나쁜 행동이에요. '표절하다'는 남의 글이나 작품을 베껴 자기 것으로 내는 것이고, 도용하다는 이름이나 카드처럼 신분과 권리까지 몰래 쓰는 데에 더 자주 써요. 실제 대화에서는 '몰래 쓰다'라고도 해요.
explain_en: Doyonghada is the wrongful act of using someone's name, card, photo, or idea as your own without permission. 표절하다 is copying another person's writing or work and presenting it as yours, whereas 도용하다 is used more for identity and rights, like names and cards. In ordinary talk people also say 몰래 쓰다.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 저와 다른 부류의 사람이에요.
examples.en: That friend is a different type of person from me.
I sorted the books by category.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 두 부류로 나눌 수 있어요.
examples.en: This problem can be divided into two types.
It's comfortable when people of the same type gather.
He is the type who doesn't talk much.
Check which category it belongs to.

explain: 부류는 성질이나 특징이 비슷한 것들을 묶어서 나눈 한 무리를 가리켜요. 사람에게 쓰면 '저런 부류의 사람'처럼 약간 평가하는 느낌이 있어서 조심해서 써야 해요. 물건이나 생각을 구별할 때는 '종류'나 '유형'이 더 중립적이에요.
explain_en: Buryu is a group of things or people with similar traits. Used for people, as in 저런 부류의 사람, it carries a hint of judgement, so be careful. For objects and ideas, 종류 and 유형 are more neutral.

examples.en: I got sick from exhaustion of my energy.
The project stopped because the budget ran out.
Burnout is called exhaustion of the mind.
The discount lasts only until stock runs out.
I was so worn out that I took a day off.

examples.ko: 자원 소진을 막기 위해 아껴 써야 해요.
examples.en: We have to use things sparingly to prevent depletion of resources.

explain: 소진은 가진 힘, 돈, 물건이 다 써서 바닥나는 것을 말해요. 안내문에서는 '재고 소진 시까지', '예산 소진'처럼 쓰고, 사람의 상태를 말할 때는 '번아웃'과 비슷한 '탈진' 느낌이에요. 말로 할 때는 '다 떨어지다', '바닥나다'가 훨씬 자연스러워요.
explain_en: Sojin means running out of strength, money, or goods until nothing is left. Notices use it in phrases like 재고 소진 시까지 and 예산 소진, and for people it is close to burnout or 탈진. In speech, 다 떨어지다 and 바닥나다 are far more natural.

examples.en: This year's budget has all been used up.

examples.ko: 하루 일을 마치니 체력이 다 소진됐어요.
examples.en: After finishing the day's work, my energy was completely drained.

examples.ko: 인기 상품은 며칠 만에 소진될 거예요.
examples.en: Popular items will run out within a few days.
The coupons ran out quickly, so I couldn't get one.
Charge it before the battery runs out.
I rested for a week to recover my depleted energy.

explain: 소진되다는 힘, 예산, 재고처럼 쓰는 것이 자연스럽게 모두 줄어서 없어질 때 써요. 내가 일부러 다 쓴 게 아니라 '그렇게 되었다'는 느낌이에요. 일상 대화에서는 '다 떨어졌어요'가 더 흔하고, 공지나 뉴스에서 소진되다를 자주 봐요.
explain_en: Sojindoeda is used when energy, budget, or stock gradually gets fully used up, as a state that came about rather than something you did on purpose. In daily talk 다 떨어졌어요 is more common, while notices and news often use 소진되다.

examples.ko: 올해 안에 휴가를 모두 소진해야 해요.
examples.en: I have to use up all my vacation days this year.
He used up all his strength in the marathon.

examples.ko: 회사는 남은 예산을 소진하려고 행사를 열었어요.
examples.en: The company held an event to use up the remaining budget.
Take a break in the middle so you don't drain your energy.

examples.ko: 재고를 소진하는 데 한 달이 걸렸어요.
examples.en: It took a month to clear out the stock.

examples.ko: 연차를 다 소진하고 나니 쉴 날이 없어요.
examples.en: Now that I've used up all my leave, I have no days off.

explain: 소진하다는 가진 시간, 힘, 연차, 예산을 일부러 또는 끝까지 써서 없앤다는 뜻이에요. '연차를 소진하다'는 직장에서 휴가를 다 쓴다는 말로 많이 들어요. 일부러 쓰는 쪽은 소진하다, 저절로 없어지는 쪽은 소진되다로 구별해요.
explain_en: Sojinhada means to use up all of what you have, such as time, energy, leave, or budget, actively or all the way to the end. 연차를 소진하다 is a common workplace phrase for using all your leave. Doing it yourself is 소진하다, and running out by itself is 소진되다.

examples.en: A rainbow is a spectrum of light.
This film covers a wide range of emotions.
That singer has a broad musical range.

examples.ko: 정치 스펙트럼이 다른 사람들과도 대화해 봤어요.
examples.en: I've talked with people from different parts of the political spectrum.

examples.ko: 넓은 스펙트럼의 책을 읽으면 생각도 넓어져요.
examples.en: Reading books across a wide spectrum broadens your thinking too.
We observed a spectrum in science class.

explain: 스펙트럼은 과학에서는 빛을 색깔별로 나눈 띠를 말하고, 일상에서는 '넓은 스펙트럼'처럼 어떤 것이 다룰 수 있는 범위를 비유로 말할 때 써요. '범위'보다 서로 다른 것들이 이어져 있는 폭이라는 느낌이 있어요. 참고로 '스펙'이라는 말은 취업 준비에서 쓰는 '조건'이라서 이 단어와는 달라요.
explain_en: Seupekteureom is, in science, a band of light split by colour, and in daily life a figurative range, as in a wide spectrum. It suggests a continuous spread of different things rather than just a 범위. Note that 스펙, used in job hunting for credentials, is a different word.

examples.en: My phone's screen cracked.
I was surprised at how expensive the screen repair was.
I put on a new screen protector.

examples.ko: 햇빛 때문에 액정이 잘 안 보여요.
examples.en: I can't see the screen well because of the sunlight.
This monitor has a sharp screen.
There are lots of fingerprints on the screen.

explain: 액정은 원래 액정 디스플레이(LCD)의 줄임말이지만, 한국에서는 휴대폰이나 TV의 화면 부분을 두루 가리키는 말로 써요. 휴대폰 화면이 깨졌을 때 '액정이 나갔다', '액정이 깨졌다'고도 말해요. 수리점에서는 '액정 교체'라는 말을 들을 수 있어요.
explain_en: Aekjeong is originally short for liquid-crystal display, but in Korea it commonly means the screen part of a phone or TV. When a phone screen breaks, people also say 액정이 나갔다 or 액정이 깨졌다. At repair shops you may hear 액정 교체.

examples.en: This word was derived from a Sino-Korean word.
Several problems branch off from a single problem.
A film spun off from that drama came out.
Many conflicts are derived from misunderstandings.
This technology grew out of military research.

examples.ko: 새로운 의미가 파생될 때 사전에 추가돼요.
examples.en: When a new meaning arises, it is added to the dictionary.

explain: 파생되다는 원래 있던 것에서 갈라져 나와 새로운 것이 생길 때 써요. 언어에서는 '파생어'처럼 하나의 말에서 새 말이 만들어지는 것을 말하고, 일반적으로는 하나의 사건에서 다른 문제가 따라 나오는 것에도 써요. '생기다'보다 원래 것과 이어져 있다는 점이 분명해요.
explain_en: Pasaengdoeda is used when something new comes out of an original, as in language, where 파생어 is a word formed from another. In general use, it also covers new problems following from one event. Unlike plain 생기다, it makes clear the new thing is connected to the original.

examples.en: Grandmother smiled as she recalled her youth.
Looking back on my childhood warms my heart.

examples.ko: 그는 전쟁 때 일을 천천히 회상했어요.
examples.en: He slowly recalled what happened during the war.

examples.ko: 옛 친구들을 회상하다 보니 눈물이 났어요.
examples.en: Thinking back on old friends, I teared up.
I wrote a blog post recalling the trip.

examples.ko: 지난 일을 회상해 보니 후회되는 게 많아요.
examples.en: Looking back on the past, there is a lot I regret.

explain: 회상하다는 지난 일을 천천히 떠올리며 되새기는 것이에요. '기억하다'는 잊지 않고 있는 것이고, '생각나다'는 저절로 떠오르는 것인데, 회상하다는 스스로 지난 시간으로 돌아가 보는 느낌이에요. 말할 때보다 글이나 이야기 속에서 더 많이 써요.
explain_en: Hoesanghada is slowly bringing past events to mind and reflecting on them. 기억하다 is not having forgotten, and 생각나다 is when a thought comes to you on its own, while 회상하다 is deliberately going back through earlier time. It appears more in writing and storytelling than in casual speech.

examples.en: Many people suffered during the period of Japanese occupation.

examples.ko: 할아버지는 강점기 시절 이야기를 해 주셨어요.
examples.en: My grandfather told me stories from the occupation period.
This building was built during the occupation period.
We learned about the occupation period in history class.
I visited a museum that collects records from the occupation era.
The independence fighters kept fighting throughout the occupation.

explain: 강점기는 다른 나라가 힘으로 우리 땅을 차지하고 있던 시기를 말하고, 한국에서는 거의 '일제 강점기'라는 형태로만 들어요. 예전에는 '일제 시대'라고도 했는데, 지금은 침략의 의미가 분명한 강점기가 학교와 뉴스에서 더 흔해요. 1910년부터 1945년까지를 가리켜요.
explain_en: Gangjeomgi is a period when another country held one's land by force, and in Korea it is nearly always heard as 일제 강점기. It was once called 일제 시대, but 강점기, which makes the aggression clear, is now more common in schools and news. It refers to the years from 1910 to 1945.

examples.en: There are bodyguards beside the president.
The singer arrived at the airport with bodyguards.
The bodyguard made the fans step back.

examples.ko: 형은 경호원이 되려고 운동을 열심히 해요.
examples.en: My brother exercises hard to become a bodyguard.
A security guard checked the bags at the event entrance.
A bodyguard's eyes are always scanning the surroundings.

explain: 경호원은 중요한 사람을 위험에서 지키는 사람이에요. 건물이나 가게를 지키는 사람은 '경비원', '보안 요원'이라고 해서 달라요. 정치인이나 연예인 같은 특정한 사람 옆에서 지킬 때 경호원이라고 해요.
explain_en: A gyeonghowon protects an important person from danger. Someone guarding a building or shop is a 경비원 or 보안 요원, which is different. 경호원 is used for those who stay beside specific people such as politicians or celebrities.
